869.title: Cranmer's hand
869.hook: after recanting, he recants his recantation and puts the hand that signed into the fire first
869.howItsDone: Anglicans and other Protestants remember Thomas Cranmer as a martyr and as the main shaper of the Book of Common Prayer, and the story of his hand in the fire is often retold from Foxe's Book of Martyrs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Book of Common Prayer, and a collect that asks God to cleanse the thoughts of our hearts. Did you say it, or read it, before something hard? Day eight hundred sixty-nine.

An old man stands in a church in Oxford, in front of a crowd. He has been in prison a long time. He is the archbishop who gave England its prayer book, and he has since signed papers taking all of it back: accepting the pope, accepting the teaching he once argued against. The crowd has been told what to expect. He will read one more statement of regret, and then he will be burned anyway. He starts to speak. He asks for prayers. He talks about the world, about money, about obeying the queen. And then he reaches the part about his writings, and the speech goes somewhere nobody planned. Today: Cranmer's hand.
screen: `AN OLD MAN IN A CHURCH IN OXFORD.`

segments.voice: Here's how he got there. When Henry's son Edward died, Mary became queen, Catherine of Aragon's daughter. She brought England back to the Catholic faith and back under Rome. Cranmer was the man who had declared her mother's marriage void. He was tried for heresy and kept in prison, and under that pressure he signed recantations. Even so, he was still sent to the stake. The story of the end is told by John Foxe, a Protestant writer who collected the stories of those Mary burned. Foxe has a side, and readers weigh his telling with that in mind. In Foxe's account, Cranmer says the papers he signed were written against the truth in his heart, out of fear of death. And since his hand had offended by writing them, his hand would be punished first. Then, at the stake, Foxe says, he stretched his right hand into the flames and held it there before the fire reached the rest of him. Some readers think of Peter here. On the night Jesus was arrested, Peter sat warming himself at a fire and swore he didn't know him. Then the rooster crowed, and in the King James Bible, "he went out, and wept bitterly." Later, by another fire on a beach, the risen Jesus gave him a way back. Christians remember Cranmer in more than one way. Protestants honor him as a martyr and as the voice of the prayer book. Catholics remember the archbishop who helped break England from Rome. Either way, the story ends with a frightened man who, at the very end, stopped hiding what he thought.

Here's the practice: own one past mistake, plainly. This isn't about punishing yourself. Settle, and breathe. Look at your own hand for a moment. Let it bring something to mind: a message it typed, a thing it signed, a door it shut. Name the mistake in one plain sentence, no excuses attached. Then let your hand rest open on your knee. If you pray, you can hand it to God with your palm open. If you don't, just notice what it's like to say it straight. The bell holds the time.
Cranmer's hand. The hand that signed his recantations, which, in John Foxe's account, he held in the fire first, owning his mistake before he died.
Your line: this hand first. Today, when something goes wrong and part of it is yours, say so first, before anyone else has to. Day eight hundred sixty-nine.

870.title: Thomas More
870.hook: the king's good servant, but God's first, executed for refusing the oath
870.howItsDone: Catholics honor Thomas More as a saint and martyr, keeping his feast together with John Fisher's, and he is honored as a patron of statesmen and politicians; Anglicans and others also remember him for his conscience.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cranmer's hand, held in the fire before the rest of him. Your line was this hand first. What did you own, plainly, before anyone had to ask? Day eight hundred seventy.

There's a portrait of him, painted in his lifetime. A dark coat trimmed with fur. A heavy gold chain across his shoulders, the mark of a man in the king's service. A face that looks clever and a little tired. Lawyer. Writer of a book called Utopia. Friend of the king, and for a time Lord Chancellor of England. Under the fine coat, tradition says, he wore a rough shirt of hair against his skin, to keep himself humble. Then the king broke with Rome, and asked for an oath. And the man in the gold chain went quiet. Today: Thomas More.
screen: `A GOLD CHAIN AND A FUR COAT.`

segments.voice: More stepped down as chancellor as Henry pulled the church in England away from Rome. Then came the oath. Leading men of the realm were asked to swear to Henry's new marriage and the new order behind it. More, as the usual account goes, was willing to accept who would inherit the crown, but he would not swear to words that set aside the pope's authority over the church. He refused, and he also refused to say why. He hoped silence would protect him, since he had said nothing against the king. He was sent to the Tower of London. His daughter Margaret visited him there and begged him to give way. He didn't. In the end he was tried, convicted on testimony he said was false, and beheaded. Tradition reports that on the scaffold he said he died the king's good servant, but God's first. Notice the order of those words. He doesn't call himself the king's enemy. He calls himself the king's servant, and a good one. He just won't put the king first. Peter and the apostles, ordered by the council in Jerusalem to stop preaching, said it in the King James Bible: "We ought to obey God rather than men." Catholics honor More as a saint and a martyr of conscience. There is more to remember. As chancellor, More pursued Protestants hard. He wrote fierce books against William Tyndale, and some of the people he hunted as heretics were burned. The story holds both pieces of the man. Brave and hard, holy and fierce. A conscience that would not bend for a king, and a chancellor who pressed hard on the consciences of others.
screen: `HE REFUSES THE OATH, AND STAYS SILENT.`
`THE KING'S GOOD SERVANT, BUT GOD'S FIRST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep your first loyalty clear. Settle, and breathe. Name, quietly, the things that ask for your loyalty: work, family, friends, a team, a country, a cause, a faith. Don't rank them yet. Just let them line up. Then ask: if two of these ever pulled against each other, which one would I keep? Don't argue with the answer. Just hear it. If you pray, you can bring that question to God and stay with it. If you don't, just let it settle in you. The bell holds the time.
Thomas More. Lawyer, writer and chancellor of England, executed for refusing Henry's oath, remembered as saying he died the king's good servant, but God's first.
Your line: god's first. Today, when two loyalties pull at you, notice which one you reach for first, and whether you'd choose it again. Day eight hundred seventy.

871.title: Burnings on both sides
871.hook: Mary burned Protestants; Elizabeth executed Catholics; both called it faithfulness
871.howItsDone: Anglicans and other Protestants remember those burned under Mary, often through Foxe's Book of Martyrs, while Catholics honor the English and Welsh martyrs of Elizabeth's reign as saints; some churches now hold services that remember both together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Thomas More: the king's good servant, but God's first. Your line was god's first. When two loyalties pulled at you, which did you reach for? Day eight hundred seventy-one.

In the middle of a street in Oxford, a small cross is set into the road. It's easy to walk over it without looking down. It marks the place where Protestants were burned, Cranmer among them. In London, near where the old Tyburn gallows stood, Catholics keep the memory of priests and laypeople who were hanged there. Two places. Two sets of the dead. The same country. Each side honored its own martyrs, and each side had killed the other's. Today: burnings on both sides.

Under Queen Mary, England went back to Rome, and Protestants who would not return were tried for heresy and burned. Hugh Latimer and Nicholas Ridley, both bishops, were burned together at Oxford. John Foxe reports that Latimer told his friend to be of good comfort and play the man, because together they would light such a candle in England as, he trusted, would never be put out. Then Mary died, and her sister Elizabeth became queen, the daughter of Anne Boleyn. The prayer book came back. Now Catholic priests, trained abroad, slipped into England in secret to say Mass in private houses. The law called them traitors. Priests were hanged, drawn and quartered, and people who sheltered them could die too. In York, Margaret Clitherow, a butcher's wife who hid priests in her home, was pressed to death. Edmund Campion, a Jesuit priest, was executed at Tyburn, and accounts of his death say he prayed for the queen who had condemned him. And both sides called it faithfulness. Mary's courts saw heresy as a poison that could kill souls forever. Elizabeth's courts saw a priest from Rome as a threat to the crown. Each side was sure it was protecting something holy. And each side was reading the same Gospel, where Jesus says, in the King James Bible: "By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another." Christians on each side still honor their own martyrs. Some, today, have begun to remember the other side's martyrs too, and to say two words the story leaves behind: never again.

Here's the practice: someone across a divide. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind people on the other side of a line that matters to you. Politics, faith, family, an old quarrel. Then do what the two sets of martyrs never got from each other: name one thing those people hold dear, something they would hate to lose. You don't have to agree with them, or excuse anything. Just wish them good: safety, rest, the thing they love kept safe. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. If you don't, just hold them kindly for a while. The bell holds the time.
Burnings on both sides. Under Mary, Protestants burned; under Elizabeth, Catholics hanged. Each side called it faithfulness, and each was reading the same Gospel.
Your line: never again. Today, when you hear someone on the other side made into a monster, stop and say one true, human thing about them. Day eight hundred seventy-one.

872.title: The Council of Trent (1545–63)
872.hook: Catholics reform seminaries, clarify teaching, and renew the Mass
872.howItsDone: Catholics receive the Council of Trent's decrees as the teaching of an ecumenical council; seminaries for training priests, which the council called for, remain the usual path to the Catholic priesthood, and the Tridentine Mass is still celebrated in some places.

segments.voice: Yesterday, burnings on both sides, and a line the story leaves for us: never again. Who across a divide did you wish well, or say one human thing about? Day eight hundred seventy-two.

What, exactly, does the Catholic Church teach, and what in its own life needs fixing? That question has been tearing the Western church apart. To answer it, bishops arrive in a city in the mountains of northern Italy, where the road climbs toward the Alps, along with theologians and representatives of kings, their servants, their books and their arguments. The council opens. Then it breaks off. Then it meets again, and breaks off again, and meets again, over long years and more than one pope. The city's name is Trent. Today's word is the name later given to the whole movement around it: Counter-Reformation.

Start with the name. Counter-Reformation sounds like a punch thrown back, and part of Trent was exactly that: an answer to Luther, Zwingli and Calvin. Some historians prefer another name, the Catholic Reformation, because some Catholics had been calling for reform of their own church before anyone left it, and because much of what Trent did was cleaning house. So it did two things at once. First, it said clearly what Catholics hold. Scripture and tradition, received together. The sacraments, defined one by one. How a person is made right with God: by grace, received in faith, and lived out in works. Protestant churches answered much of this differently; Catholics receive these decrees as the teaching of a general council of the church. Second, it turned inward. Bishops were told to live in their own dioceses and preach, instead of collecting income from far away. Each diocese was to have a seminary, a school where future priests would be trained before they were sent to a parish. And after the council came a catechism and a single form of the Mass for much of the Latin church, which people still call the Tridentine Mass, from Trent. Paul writes, in the King James Bible: "be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind." Trent is what renewal looks like when a large, old institution tries it on itself: slowly, with arguments, interrupted, and then carried out into the parishes by priests who had been trained first.

Here's the practice: one thing Trent did well. Settle, and breathe. Take one of its quieter changes: bishops were told to live among the people they served, instead of drawing an income from far away. Bring to mind one thing you look after from a distance. A friendship kept up only by text. A group you belong to on paper. A place or a person you're meant to care for. What would it mean to show up there in person this week? Choose one small step. If you pray, you can ask for help to take it. If you don't, just hold the step in mind and let it settle. The bell holds the time.

Counter-Reformation. The name later given to the Catholic answer to the Reformation, centered on the Council of Trent, which both restated Catholic teaching and reformed the church's own life. Some call it the Catholic Reformation.
Your line: reform from within. Today, instead of walking away from one thing that's broken, fix one small part of it from the inside. Day eight hundred seventy-two.

873.title: Ignatius' cannonball
873.hook: a soldier's leg is shattered, and bored in bed he reads lives of saints
873.howItsDone: Catholics honor Ignatius of Loyola as a saint and as founder of the Jesuits; people of many churches make his Spiritual Exercises on retreats, and some end each day with a short review of which moments left them consoled or empty.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Council of Trent and the Counter-Reformation, a church trying to fix itself. Your line was reform from within. What small broken thing did you fix from the inside? Day eight hundred seventy-three.

A fortress wall in Pamplona, in the north of Spain, under siege. The other defenders want to surrender. One young Basque nobleman talks them into fighting on. His name is Iñigo, and he loves fine clothes, swordplay and stories of knights. Then a cannonball comes over the wall and smashes his leg. The fortress falls. His enemies carry him home on a litter to his family's castle at Loyola. Surgeons set the leg badly, and it has to be broken and set again. A bone still juts out below the knee, and, by his own later account, he has it sawed off so the leg will look right in a close-fitting boot. Then there's nothing left to do but lie in bed. Today: Ignatius' cannonball.
screen: `NOTHING TO DO BUT LIE IN BED.`

segments.voice: Bored, he asks for something to read. He wants romances about knights and their ladies. The house doesn't have any. What it has is a life of Christ and a book of the lives of the saints. So he reads those, because there's nothing else. And here's what he noticed, later telling it about himself in the third person, calling himself the pilgrim. His mind kept switching between two daydreams. In one, he was a knight again, winning glory and the favor of a great lady. In the other, he was doing what Francis and Dominic did, walking barefoot, giving everything away. Both daydreams were pleasant while they lasted. But afterward, the knight daydream left him dry and restless, and the saint daydream left him quiet and content. He began to pay attention to that difference. Which thoughts leave you consoled? Which leave you empty? That small noticing in a sickbed became the root of what Jesuits call discernment, and of the Spiritual Exercises he would later write, a set of meditations people still make on retreats. When he could walk again, the soldier left his sword before an image of Mary, by his own account, and went off as a beggar and a pilgrim. Later, with friends, he founded the Society of Jesus, the Jesuits. Paul, in the King James Bible, hears God say: "My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness." The cannonball didn't make Ignatius holy. It made him lie still long enough to notice. Wounded into holiness doesn't mean the wound was good. It means something good came through it.

Here's the practice: someone brave. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a brave person whose story you know. A saint, a grandparent, a nurse, someone from the news, someone from a book. Let their story play for a minute. Then do what Ignatius did in bed: notice what the story leaves behind in you. Restless, or quiet? Smaller, or steadier? Don't judge it. Just notice. If you pray, you can thank God for them. If you don't, just stay with them a while. Later today, read one page about them. The bell holds the time.
Ignatius' cannonball. The shot that smashed a soldier's leg and left him in bed with nothing to read but lives of Christ and the saints, where he learned to notice which thoughts left him content.

Your line: wounded into holiness. Today, when something stops you, a delay, a cold, a canceled plan, ask what you might notice in the stillness that you'd miss at full speed. Day eight hundred seventy-three.

874.title: Xavier to Asia
874.hook: Francis Xavier sails to India, Japan, and dies on an island off China
874.carry: to the ends of the earth
874.howItsDone: Catholics honor Francis Xavier as a saint and a patron of missions, and in Goa, India, his remains are kept and venerated; Christians in Asia remember him as part of the longer story of their churches.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ignatius' cannonball, and a soldier who learned to notice in a sickbed. Your line was wounded into holiness. What did a stop in your day let you notice? Day eight hundred seventy-four.

So close he can see it. In a rough hut on a small island off the coast of China, a man lies with a fever. Through the doorway, across the water, is the mainland he has been trying to reach. Foreigners are not allowed in, and he is waiting for a trader who promised to smuggle him across. The trader doesn't come. The man in the hut dies there, far from the country where he was born, still looking at the shore. He had started out, long before, as a proud young student in Paris, sharing lodgings with an older man who walked with a limp. Today: Xavier to Asia.
screen: `A HUT ON AN ISLAND OFF CHINA.`

segments.voice: The older man with the limp was Ignatius. Francis Xavier was a gifted young Basque with plans for a fine career, and Ignatius, tradition says, kept asking him the question from the Gospel: "what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?" Eventually Xavier joined him, and became one of the founding Jesuits. Then, the story goes, when the man chosen to go east fell ill, Xavier was sent in his place, almost overnight. He sailed from Portugal on a Portuguese ship, around Africa, to Goa in India. He walked the fishing villages of the southern coast, and with helpers he put prayers and teachings into the local language. Accounts say he walked the streets ringing a small bell to call children to learn. Later he went on to Japan, where he found he had to change his ways: to learn courtesy, to dress for respect, to argue patiently with people who asked hard questions. Then he set his heart on China, and got as far as that island. In Acts, Paul and Barnabas quote the Lord's command to be "for salvation unto the ends of the earth." Xavier took that line literally. There's a harder side too. He traveled on the ships of an empire, and mission and empire were tangled together in ways that Christians in Asia, and historians, still talk about. Catholics honor him as a saint and a patron of missions. And he was not the first Christian in India: the Thomas Christians of the southwest coast trace their church to the apostle Thomas, long before any Portuguese ship. Asian Christians tell their own stories, which carried on long after the visitor was gone.

Here's the practice: hold Asia in mind. Settle, and breathe. Picture a map, and let your attention travel east the way Xavier's ship did. The coast of India, with its fishing villages. The islands of Japan. The long shore of China. Then let the map fill with people: anyone you know there, or whose family comes from there, a coworker, a neighbor, a friend. Let their faces come. If you pray, you can pray for them, and for the churches and peoples of Asia. If you don't, just wish them well, one by one. The bell holds the time.
Xavier to Asia. Francis Xavier, a friend of Ignatius, who sailed to India and Japan and died on an island off China, still trying to reach the mainland.
Your line: to the ends of the earth. Today, reach one person who feels far away from you, by distance or by difference, with a message, a call, or a kind word. Day eight hundred seventy-four.

875.title: Teresa's reform
875.hook: Teresa founds small, poor, joyful convents on dusty roads
875.tomorrow: John of the Cross in prison
875.howItsDone: Discalced Carmelite nuns still live in small enclosed communities shaped by Teresa's reform, and her short poem beginning "let nothing disturb you" is prayed and sung by Catholics and others, often as a short repeated chant.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Xavier to Asia, dying within sight of China. Your line was to the ends of the earth. Who far away did you reach, by distance or by difference? Day eight hundred seventy-five.

The convent had a parlor, and the parlor was busy. Friends dropped by. Relatives brought news. Nuns from good families kept their comforts, and talked through the grille with visitors for hours. One of those nuns, in the Spanish city of Ávila, was witty, warm, and very good company, and she enjoyed the parlor as much as anyone. She later wrote that, for a long stretch of her life, her prayer was half-hearted, pulled between God and the world. Then something in her turned, and she began to want something much smaller and much simpler. Her name was Teresa. Today: Teresa's reform.

Teresa's idea was simple. A small house. Only a handful of sisters. Poor, living on what was given. Enclosed, so the parlor wouldn't run the day. Simple habits, and sandals instead of shoes, which is why her nuns came to be called discalced, meaning unshod. Time for silent prayer every day. And joy: she wanted her sisters cheerful, not grim. Her first small house in Ávila met fierce opposition from the town and from her own order. She opened it anyway. Then she went out on the roads of Spain, in rough covered carts, through heat and dust and mud, founding more houses. There's a story people tell from those journeys. Thrown from a cart into a muddy river, she complained to God, and heard that this is how he treats his friends. Her answer: no wonder you have so few. Whether or not it happened, it sounds like her. Teresa wasn't only an organizer. She wrote about prayer as a journey inward through a castle of many rooms, with God at the center. And among her papers, tradition says, was found a short poem. In English it goes something like this: let nothing disturb you, let nothing frighten you; all things are passing, God does not change; patience gains everything; whoever has God lacks nothing; God alone is enough. It sounds like what Jesus told a busy Martha, in the King James Bible: "Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things: But one thing is needful." The Catholic Church names Teresa a saint and a Doctor of the Church. She is a reformer who made things smaller, so there would be room for the one thing.

Here's the practice: simplify one routine. Settle, and breathe. Pick one ordinary routine: your morning, your phone before bed, the way you leave the house, the way you start work. Walk through it slowly in your mind. Notice the steps that crowd it. Then imagine doing it with one thing fewer, the way Teresa cut a convent down to its center. Don't fix it yet. Just see it. If you pray, you can say her line slowly: let nothing disturb you. If you don't, just let it be quiet for a moment. The bell holds the time.
Teresa's reform. Small, poor, joyful houses of prayer that Teresa of Ávila founded along the roads of Spain, cutting convent life down to its center.

Your line: let nothing disturb you. This week ran from Cranmer's hand and Thomas More, through burnings on both sides, Trent, Ignatius and Xavier, to Teresa. Today, take one thing out of one routine, and keep it out. Day eight hundred seventy-five.

fork.setup: you're Teresa, a well-liked nun in a large, comfortable convent with a busy parlor. you want more room for prayer. what do you do?
